opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a lot, because the original AlphaGo and AlphaZero lineage, and then KataGo and Leela Zero, were all built on residual convolutional networks. And there's a really good reason for that: Go has a very strong spatial inductive bias. The board is a 19-by-19 grid, the rules are local. Whether a stone is captured depends on its liberties, which are its immediate neighbors, and shapes like eyes, ladders, and ko fights are built up from local patterns. A convolution is basically a learned local pattern detector that gets reused across every position on the board, and that matches the structure of the game almost perfectly. You get translation equivariance for free, you're very parameter efficient, and you're very compute efficient at inference time, which matters a lot when you're running thousands of MCTS simulations per move.

The weakness of convolutions is that information propagates slowly. Each layer only sees a 3-by-3 neighborhood, so to reason about something happening on the other side of the board, like a ladder that runs diagonally across the whole board, or the life and death of a big group that snakes around, you need a lot of depth before the receptive field covers it. KataGo added global pooling layers partly to patch over that, so the network can get some board-wide summary at every block.

Transformers flip the tradeoff. Self-attention is global from the first layer: every intersection can attend to every other intersection, so long-range dependencies are easy to express. The cost is that you throw away the spatial prior, and the model has to learn locality from data, usually with some kind of positional encoding to help. And attention over 361 tokens is more expensive per layer than a convolution, which hurts you in a search setting where you care about throughput.

My view is that in the regime most people are in, a moderate compute budget where you're doing self-play and training from scratch, the ResNet tends to win, or at least it's very hard to beat, because the inductive bias does so much work for you. When you scale up data and compute, the transformer's flexibility starts to pay off, and the general lesson from deep learning, the bitter lesson in a sense, is that the less constrained architecture eventually catches up and overtakes the one with hand-designed priors. But "eventually" is doing a lot of work there. For a game like Go, where the prior is so well matched to the problem, the crossover point might be pretty far out.

Practically, I think the most interesting answer is some kind of hybrid: convolutional stems or local mixing for the cheap, local tactical stuff, plus attention or global pooling layers for whole-board reasoning. That's roughly where the field has been converging anyway. And from a research perspective, the reason I find it worth experimenting with transformers on Go isn't necessarily to beat KataGo tomorrow. It's that if you want to understand how these architectures learn to plan and search, Go is a clean testbed where you know the ground truth is very strong, and you can see exactly where the transformer struggles compared to the ResNet.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the interesting thing about Go specifically is that the inductive bias of convolutions is actually pretty well-matched to the problem. You've got a 19-by-19 board, the rules are translation-invariant in the sense that a local shape means the same thing wherever it sits, and a lot of what makes a move good is captured by local patterns: ladders, eyes, cutting points, that kind of thing. So when AlphaGo and then AlphaZero used residual conv nets, that wasn't a historical accident. The conv net is baking in a prior that the board is a spatial grid with local structure, and that prior is correct. You pay very little in terms of expressivity and you get a lot of sample efficiency back.

The problem is the stuff that isn't local. Ladders are the classic example. A ladder is a sequence of captures that can run diagonally across the whole board, and whether it works depends on a stone sitting in the far corner. A conv net with a limited receptive field has to stack a lot of layers to "see" that, and even then it's learning a very indirect representation of a long-range dependency. People saw this empirically: ladders were a known weakness in early self-play systems and you'd get these surprising blunders. So that's where the transformer argument comes in. Attention gives you global receptive field in one layer. Any position can attend to any other position, so in principle a ladder or a large-scale semeai becomes something the model can represent directly rather than having to approximate through depth.

But my view is that the tradeoff isn't really "which architecture is better," it's "where is your compute going." With a conv net you spend your compute on a strong prior and you get strong play with relatively fewer games. With a transformer you've thrown away the prior and now the model has to rediscover translation invariance and locality from data. Transformers do rediscover it, we've seen that over and over in vision, but it costs you samples. And in Go the samples are self-play games, which aren't free. You're running MCTS to generate each one. So for a fixed compute budget, especially a small one, the conv net is often going to win.

Where it flips is at scale and in the regime where you care about the hard long-range stuff. Once you have enough self-play data that the prior stops mattering, the transformer's flexibility starts paying off, and you also get the nice property that the same architecture works if you change the board size or want to transfer to a different game. KataGo, for instance, got a lot of mileage out of fairly clever conv-net tricks for global information, like global pooling layers that broadcast a summary of the whole board back into the local features. That's kind of a poor man's attention. And honestly that approach was so effective that it's not obvious the full transformer buys you much for Go in particular.

So the way I'd frame it: the conv net is the right answer when your bottleneck is data, the transformer is the right answer when your bottleneck is the architecture's ability to express the thing you need, and for Go the honest answer is that you're usually data-bottlenecked, which is why resnets held on so long there compared to basically every other domain.

r001.rationale: The response says attention gives transformers a global receptive field and that flexibility can pay off at scale, but it does not state that transformers generally outperform residual convolutional networks when global context is needed. It also says the advantage for Go is unclear and conv nets often win under fixed compute.

astra-6.text:
I think the tradeoff is really about inductive bias versus flexibility. With a residual convolutional network, you’re building in the assumption that local patterns matter and that a useful pattern in one part of the board is probably useful elsewhere. That’s a pretty good assumption for Go, although edges and corners behave differently. It gives you a very efficient way to learn from a finite amount of data.

A transformer can connect any two positions directly. That’s appealing because Go also involves these long-range relationships: whether a group is alive can depend on what’s happening across the board. A convolutional network can represent those relationships too, but it has to build them up through successive layers.

So I wouldn’t say that attention is automatically better because Go requires global reasoning. The question is whether that flexibility pays for its computational cost. In a system that uses tree search, a cheaper network might let you evaluate more positions, and that can matter more than making each individual evaluation a little better. You want to compare the strength of the whole system at a fixed compute budget, rather than just compare the architectures in isolation.

r001.rationale: The response notes that transformers can connect distant positions, but it does not say they generally outperform residual convolutional networks when global context is needed. It cautions that attention is not automatically better and frames the tradeoff around compute.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention KataGo or explain that aggregating global features throughout its network connects value across distant parts of the board.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main tradeoff is how much structure you build into the architecture versus how much you ask it to learn. A convolutional network has a useful prior for Go: the same local pattern can matter in different places on the board, so you share weights across positions. With enough residual layers, information can propagate across the board and you can reason about global relationships.

A transformer lets positions interact directly through attention. That’s attractive because Go has these very nonlocal dependencies—a move in one corner can affect whether a group elsewhere is alive. But you’re giving up some of the spatial bias that makes convolutions efficient, unless you put it back through positional information or a hybrid architecture.

So I wouldn’t assume that a transformer wins just because it’s more general. On a fixed-size board, with a particular training and inference budget, a residual convolutional network can be a very strong choice. And in Go, inference cost matters twice: you want a good policy and value estimate, but you also want to evaluate lots of positions during search. A more expressive network has to earn back the search you lose by making each evaluation more expensive.

r001.rationale: The response notes transformers' direct attention and Go's nonlocal dependencies, but it does not state that transformers generally outperform residual convolutional networks when more global context is needed. It instead says not to assume transformers win.
